name: Overnight lip/eye masks

lead: Overnight lip and eye masks are thick balms, gels or sheets applied before bed and left on while you sleep. People use them to wake up with softer, less dry lips and a smoother, more hydrated look around the eyes.

They work on ordinary moisturiser principles: occlusives such as petrolatum form a film that slows water loss, and humectants attract water. The effect is on hydration and the look of dryness and fine lines, not on structure, and it is visible by morning. No clinical trials of these specific masks were found.

paras: Users apply a layer to lips or the skin around the eyes as the last step of a night routine and wipe it off in the morning. Lips are often exfoliated gently first. Many use them nightly, especially in dry weather.
Irritation or allergic contact dermatitis from fragrance or other ingredients is possible. Paraffin-based products are flammable. Eye-area products should be kept out of the eyes.

angle.text: Thick lip and eye masks left on overnight keep skin moisturised, so lips wake up softer and the eye area looks smoother and less dry. The effect is visible by morning and comes from ordinary occlusive and humectant moisturising.

lead: Overnight lip and eye masks are leave-on products, usually a thick balm, gel or sheet, applied before bed and left on while sleeping. They are marketed to moisturise the lips and the thin skin around the eyes and to soften the look of dryness and fine lines by morning.

Most work on general moisturiser principles: occlusives such as petrolatum form a film that slows water loss, and humectants attract water.[1] Sleep masks that cover the eyes are a separate product, used to block light.[2] No clinical trial of these specific overnight masks was located.

paras: Products range from petrolatum- or wax-based lip balms to gel or hydrogel under-eye patches and creamy eye masks. Ointments are more occlusive than creams, which are more occlusive than lotions.[1]

Occlusives cut transepidermal water loss; a petrolatum layer can reduce it by roughly half to three-quarters for several hours.[1] Humectants draw in water but can leave deeper layers drier unless paired with an occlusive.[1] Light-blocking fabric sleep masks, which are a different item, are described as helping deeper sleep.[2]
Moisturisers can cause contact dermatitis from fragrances or other ingredients, and 'hypoallergenic' is not a regulated term.[1] Paraffin-based products are a fire hazard near open flames.[1]
